proposals.relationship: Greer criticizes Innis’s trade-centred conception of the colonial economy for obscuring household production and subsistence work.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1985:9 and 20–21 explicitly distinguishes Innis’s exchange focus from Pentland’s production relations, then argues that their colonial economy excludes much household output. Creighton is a joint target at 9. This is Greer’s specified methodological criticism, not independently verified output estimates, denial of every Innis contribution, or a fresh reading of Innis’s books. Existing group critique edge_1013 remains intact.

proposals.relationship: Greer includes Creighton in his criticism of staples history for concentrating on exchange rather than social production.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1985:9 names Innis, Creighton and their contemporary followers together. The contrast credits Pentland’s attention to production relations while criticizing his trade-centred categories. It is not a wholesale assessment of Creighton’s career or a fresh reading of The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence. The later household-production discussion supports the scope, without assigning every later sentence specifically to Creighton.

proposals.relationship: Greer uses Marx’s reading of Wakefield to distinguish capitalist dispossession from the claim that colonial land policy alone could remake society.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1985:21/note 22 expressly approves Marx’s use of Wakefield as a revealing bourgeois admission rather than a practicable programme. The reference is Capital, Moscow 1954, volume 1, chapter 33; its edition/translation and original chapter are not newly read. This particular argumentative resource is distinct from generic Marxist identity. Earlier 10 contrasts Marx/Engels’s broad class relations with Pentland’s ladder of stages and retains their joint conceptual credit.

proposals.relationship: Greer uses Van Kirk’s history of women in the fur trade to expose the gender bias of equating labour with salaried male work.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1985:20 explicitly credits Van Kirk before arguing that a focus on wage labour writes productive women out of the household economy. Note 19 cites Many Tender Ties, Winnipeg 1980. This is a specific historical resource for his critique, not mentorship or a new reading of Van Kirk’s original. Greer’s claims about aggregate subsistence output remain his unreplicated argument.

proposals.relationship: Greer uses Benton’s account of maritime and uneven sovereignty to distinguish early modern empire from territorial colonization.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2018:5–6 explicitly credits Benton and others, citing A Search for Sovereignty (2010) in notes 13–14 and 16. Subrahmanyam, Bertrand, Stoler and Maier retain their separate supporting roles; Benton is not sole origin. This conceptual use supports his correction of Said’s land-centred formulation. The original Benton book and other cited works remain unread here.

proposals.relationship: Greer challenges Cronon’s description of colonial land as capital when arguing for the limited role of capitalism in early North American property formation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2018:3/note 6 quotes Changes in the Land (1983),77, as an influential example, then 3–4 stresses residence, subsistence and settler commons. This is a particular periodization/interpretation objection, not rejection of Cronon’s whole ecological history or independent reading of the original book. Dispossession and exploitation are retained rather than made benign.

proposals.relationship: Greer qualifies Said’s land-possession definition of empire, arguing that it better describes colonization than early modern imperial reach.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2018:5–6 quotes Culture and Imperialism, cited in the 1994 Knopf manifestation,78, and proposes replacing empire with colonization in that formulation. Benton’s maritime and nodal account is a positive resource. This is a narrow early modern conceptual correction, not a wholesale dismissal of Said or a newly read original. Spanish conquest and uneven American territorial control remain differentiated.

proposals.relationship: Greer adapts Arendt’s property–wealth distinction to explain how household-based colonial property could be expansive and dispossessing without being chiefly profit-driven.
proposals.evidence_note: Own publisher HTML, section Property Formation in Comparative Perspective, explicitly uses and modifies Arendt’s distinction. Note 50 identifies The Human Condition (Chicago 1958) and the named private-realm/property and property/wealth sections; the original is unread and its organization is not independently collated. Greer differs from Arendt’s postwar diagnosis and expressly refuses a benign or egalitarian reading of settler households. No printed paragraph page is invented from unpaginated HTML.
primary_locators: Greer2018 introduction, section Property Formation in Comparative Perspective, Arendt paragraph/note50

proposals.relationship: Greer adopts Wolfe’s critique of naturalized settler history and continuing dispossession while seeking a more differentiated colonial chronology.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2019:62–63 explicitly calls for taking on board Wolfe’s historiographical critique, developed further by Veracini, and values the structure-not-event formulation. Notes 2–3 and 7–8 distinguish Wolfe 2007,1999,2006 and Veracini 2010; originals remain unread here. Positive uptake coexists with Greer’s scope objection; neither automatic full agreement nor a direct personal teaching relationship is inferred.

proposals.relationship: Greer argues that Wolfe’s settlement–exploitation dyad needs extension to capture other overlapping colonial forms in northern North America.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2019:63–64 names Wolfe’s Australia/India focus, then introduces imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism as additional modes. Greer insists these coexist and overlap rather than form self-contained stages. He expressly values Wolfe’s critique and does not attribute every casual temporal flattening to Wolfe himself. Existing group critique edge_1012 remains; original Wolfe texts are unread.
primary_locators: Greer2019:63–64; note10 points to his separately unread WMQ2019 argument

proposals.relationship: Palmer criticizes the coherence of Greer and Radforth’s Colonial Leviathan while valuing its articles and reinterpretation of responsible government.
proposals.evidence_note: Complete signed review 365–367, especially 366, distinguishes this collection-level objection from his separate criticism of Bruce Curtis. Greer and Ian Radforth are joint editors, not sole authors of all chapters. Palmer credits the volume’s revision of responsible government and calls for broader synthesis; neither total dismissal nor a new reading of the 1992 collection is claimed. Existing group comparison edge_1011 keeps its original qualifications.
